title: Bell-certified retardance polarimetry from CHSH correlators
abstract: Bell-CHSH measurements with polarization-entangled photons are commonly used as nonlocality witnesses. Here we show that the same coincidence data can also provide a quantitative metrological certificate for optical retardance sensing. For a local birefringent phase encoded on one photon, we derive the classical Fisher information directly from experimentally accessible CHSH correlators and obtain a lower bound expressed in terms of the measured correlations and the phase derivative of the CHSH parameter. In the unbiased-marginal two-qubit regime, the canonical CHSH analyzer settings are shown to be simultaneously Bell-optimal and Fisher-optimal, saturating the quantum Fisher information for retardance estimation in the ideal case. We further analyze reduced visibility, phase noise, analyzer misalignment, and finite coincidence counts, and construct conservative lower confidence bounds that can be evaluated without quantum-state tomography. The results also clarify that Bell violation and metrological usefulness are distinct resources: nonzero Fisher information can persist below the CHSH-violation threshold. The protocol therefore enables a standard Bell-test data set to provide both a nonlocality benchmark and a statistically controlled sensitivity certificate for quantum polarimetry.
summary: This paper shows that the coincidence measurements used to test quantum nonlocality via CHSH inequalities can simultaneously provide a quantitative measure of sensitivity for estimating an unknown phase shift (retardance). By deriving the Fisher Information directly from these correlators, the authors establish a robust, data-driven certificate for quantum polarimetry using standard Bell-test setups.
main_problem: To demonstrate that coincidence data collected during a Bell test can serve as a quantitative metrological certificate for estimating a local birefringent phase (retardance polarimetry).
main_result: The CHSH data provides a rigorous lower bound on retardance sensitivity, which is useful even when the Bell inequality is not violated. This shows that Bell violation and metrological usefulness are distinct resources.
method: The authors derive the classical Fisher Information directly from experimentally accessible CHSH correlators and establish a lower bound relating this FI to the derivative of the CHSH parameter.
model_or_system: The system involves polarization-entangled photons generated via SPDC, where one photon undergoes a local birefringent phase encoding. The analysis uses a two-outcome measurement model based on CHSH correlators.
key_observables: CHSH correlators ($E_{xy}$), the CHSH parameter ($S$), and the derived Classical Fisher Information ($F_C$).
important_parameters: The phase shift ($\phi$), visibility ($v$), and the degree of Bell violation.
main_assumptions: The certification assumes unbiased single-party marginals and relies on the measurement settings being trusted (semi-device-independent).
figures_summary: Figure 1 conceptually links the CHSH correlators, the Bell parameter, and the Fisher Information. Figure 2 shows how the FI bound behaves under visibility loss, and Figure 3 illustrates the finite-data confidence bound approaching the asymptotic limit.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by deriving the FI bound from CHSH correlators, provides mathematical appendices detailing the derivations (e.g., using Cauchy-Schwarz), and concludes by discussing the practical implications for quantum polarimetry.
why_interesting: It bridges two distinct areas of quantum physics—nonlocality testing (Bell tests) and quantum metrology—by showing that the data set for one can quantify the sensitivity for the other, which is highly relevant for experimental quantum optics.
